The Gobi Desert. A large cold desert spanning roughly five hundred thousand square miles across Mongolia and northern China, notable for its rocky terrain, sparse vegetation, and role as a major historical corridor for Silk Road trade and Mongol expansion. Despite its forbidding climate, it has supported pastoral nomadic societies and contains significant paleontological deposits.

It extends across southern Mongolia and northern China, or Inner Mongolia. The name derives from the Mongolian word for waterless place. The terrain consists primarily of gravel plains, rocky outcrops, and sparse dunes—less sandy than other major deserts. Temperatures range from extreme summer heat to subarctic winters, with winter temperatures plunging to minus forty degrees Celsius.

The Gobi is one of the coldest deserts. Snow occasionally falls, making it distinctly different from hot-desert climates. A major section of the Silk Road passed through the Gobi, connecting China with Central Asia. Oasis cities like Kashgar and Samarkand were vital trade hubs that sustained this commerce.

The Gobi is rich in paleontological discoveries. Dinosaur fossils, including the Velociraptor and early ceratopsians, have been unearthed in the Flaming Cliffs of Mongolia. The Gobi was the homeland of Mongol pastoralists for centuries. Genghis Khan and the Mongol Empire rose from the Gobi region, launching campaigns that reshaped Eurasia.

Modern mining operations extracting coal, copper, and rare earth elements have transformed parts of the Gobi economically and environmentally. The Gobi marks China's northwest frontier, with the Great Wall's terminus facing it. The desert's paleontological significance, its role in Silk Road commerce, and its place as the heartland of the Mongol Empire all underscore its importance in world history.
